screens.title: Transactions vs Queries
screens.narratorSegment: A transaction in Fabric is any operation that intends to change ledger state. From the client perspective, that means you must use submitTransaction rather than evaluateTransaction. submitTransaction initiates a coordinated lifecycle: the SDK assembles and signs a proposal, gets endorsements from peers that simulate the change, and then submits the endorsed transaction to ordering. After ordering, peers validate and commit the block. This end-to-end process gives your application assurance that the effect is durable and visible to other peers. A common misconception is that submitTransaction only sends a write request and exits. In fact, the Node. js SDK waits until peers commit the transaction and will resolve the returned Promise only after that commitment. An example use case is a CreateAsset function: you must submit a transaction so that the new asset appears in the world state across peers. Contrast this with evaluateTransaction, which is appropriate for reads, fast inspection, and does not touch ordering or block formation. When designing applications, treat submitTransaction as a synchronous checkpoint: it is your signal that the change is finalized. Remember to validate input before submission and to prepare for errors from chaincode logic or endorsement mismatches.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: submitTransaction is the SDK method to create state-changing transactions and waits for commitment, while evaluateTransaction is for read-only queries.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Transactions vs Queries
Transactions vs Queries
Understand the intent and guarantees of submitTransaction compared to evaluateTransaction.
Quick definition
  • submitTransaction: state-changing, proposal → endorsement → ordering → commit, Promise resolves after commit.
  • evaluateTransaction: read-only, simulated execution, no ordering or commit.
Concrete example
Calling CreateAsset must use submitTransaction so the new asset is stored in the world state and visible to all peers after commit.
Common misconception
Thinking submitTransaction is fire-and-forget. It waits for commit; handle errors accordingly.
Key Takeaway

Use submitTransaction for any action that must update the ledger and require commit assurance across peers.

Lifecycle overview
1. Transaction Proposal — SDK creates and signs a proposal with function and args.
2. Endorsement — endorsing peers simulate execution and return signed proposal responses.
3. Collection & Submission — Gateway gathers endorsements and sends a transaction to ordering.
4. Ordering & Block Formation — ordering service sequences transactions into blocks.
5. Commitment — peers validate and commit, updating world state.
Why this matters
Commit assurance prevents state confusion and ensures that once your app sees a successful submitTransaction, the change is durable across the channel.

screens.title: Get Network and Contract Objects
screens.narratorSegment: Before submitting any transaction you must obtain two references: a Network object representing the channel and a Contract object representing the deployed chaincode. The Gateway connection encapsulates your application identity and discovery settings. From that gateway you call gateway. getNetwork with the channel name to retrieve a Network. Then call network. getContract with the chaincode name — optionally including a contract name within the package — to get a Contract. This mapping matters because the Contract determines the available functions you can call. A common pattern is network. getContract('basic', 'myAssetContract') when using the contract A P I structure inside chaincode. If chaincode exposes functions directly without the contract A P I, you may call network. getContract('basic') and reference functions by name. Verify that the channel name and chaincode name match what was deployed; a mismatch is a frequent source of runtime errors. Practically, you will place these calls after gateway. connect in your Node. js main function and reuse the Contract instance for multiple submitTransaction and evaluateTransaction calls. This reuse reduces overhead and makes your code clearer. Always disconnect the gateway when your app completes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Get Network and Contract
Network and Contract references
These objects scope your SDK calls to a specific channel and chaincode package.
How to obtain them
  1. Establish a Gateway connection using your wallet and connection profile.
  2. Call gateway.getNetwork with your channel name to get a Network object.
  3. Call network.getContract with the chaincode package name and optional contract name to get a Contract.
Concrete code sketch
After connecting the gateway: const network = await gateway.getNetwork('mychannel'); const contract = network.getContract('basic');
Pitfall
Using the wrong chaincode or channel name results in function-not-found or runtime errors. Confirm deployment names before calling.
Key Takeaway

Obtain Network and Contract once after connecting the gateway, then reuse the Contract for multiple invocations.

Reference mapping
Gateway
Client identity, discovery, and connectivity context for the application.
Network
Represents the channel where your chaincode is deployed.
Contract
A specific chaincode package or named contract exposing functions to invoke.
Usage
Use the Contract instance to call submitTransaction or evaluateTransaction as needed.
Practical note
Reusing Contract reduces repeated lookups and simplifies your application flow. Always disconnect the gateway when done.

screens.title: submitTransaction Lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: When you call submitTransaction, the SDK triggers a multi-step lifecycle. First it creates a transaction proposal that includes the chaincode function name and arguments and signs it with your application's identity. Next, endorsing peers receive the proposal and simulate execution, producing signed proposal responses containing read/write sets. The Gateway collects the required endorsements based on the chaincode's endorsement policy. Once enough valid endorsements are collected, the Gateway packages them into a final transaction and submits it to the ordering service. The ordering service sequences transactions and forms blocks. Blocks are distributed to peers, which validate transactions by checking endorsement policy and read/write conflicts, and then commit the valid transactions to the ledger. The Node. js submitTransaction Promise resolves only after peers commit the transaction to their ledgers, providing your application with a durable success signal. A useful mental model is: proposal for simulation, endorsements as signed agreement, ordering for global sequence, and commitment for durable state change. Design your application to handle failures at each stage: endorsement errors, ordering delays, or commit rejections due to MVCC conflicts. submitTransaction Lifecycle means proposal → endorsement → collection → ordering → commitment; submittransaction coordinates these and waits for commit.. In practical terms, what the sdk and gateway do behind the scenes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › submitTransaction Lifecycle
Transaction flow the Gateway manages
Each stage has its own failure modes and recovery patterns.
1. Proposal: signed by application; contains function and args for simulation.
2. Endorsement: peers simulate and return signed responses with read/write sets.
3. Collection & Submission: Gateway gathers endorsements and sends transaction to ordering.
4. Ordering & Block Formation: ordering service sequences transactions into blocks.
5. Commitment: peers validate and commit the transaction to the ledger and world state.
Failure modes & what to check
  • Endorsement failure: not enough valid signatures per policy — check peer selection and policy.
  • Ordering delays: temporary latency; design timeouts and retries appropriately.
  • Commit conflicts: read/write set mismatch causes validation failure — implement optimistic concurrency handling.
Practical tip
For many apps, waiting for commit is safer. For very high throughput, consider asynchronous event handlers to process commit confirmations separately.
Why it matters

Understanding the lifecycle helps you design retries, user feedback, and error handling that match real network behavior.

Terminal-style code snippet
This is the pattern you'll run in app.js to submit assets.
// ... after gateway.connect()
const network = await gateway.getNetwork('mychannel');
const contract = network.getContract('basic');

console.log('
--> Submit Transaction: CreateAsset, creates new asset with ID "asset1"');
let result = await contract.submitTransaction('CreateAsset', 'asset1', 'blue', '5', 'Tom', '1000');
console.log(`*** Result: ${result.toString() || 'committed'}`);

// Update
await contract.submitTransaction('UpdateAsset', 'asset1', 'blue', '5', 'Bob', '1000');
console.log('*** Result: committed');
Note
Arguments are strings. Chaincode should parse numeric strings to integers as needed.
Handling the Buffer response
When chaincode returns data, submitTransaction resolves to a Buffer. Convert it to a string to inspect returned JSON or plain text.
const response = await contract.submitTransaction('ReadAsset', 'asset1');
console.log(response.toString());
Error handling pattern
Wrap submitTransaction in try/catch and log the error.message so expected chaincode errors are captured cleanly.
Example: Catch duplicate asset creation and present a clear message instead of allowing a crash.

screens.title: Error Handling & Common Failures
screens.narratorSegment: Robust error handling is essential when submitting transactions. There are several failure modes you will encounter. First, chaincode-level errors: if the chaincode detects invalid input or an already-existing asset, it returns an error and submitTransaction throws an exception. Your app should catch this and present a helpful message to the user. Second, endorsement policy failures occur when the collected proposal responses do not satisfy the chaincode's endorsement policy. This indicates that the Gateway could not get the required signed endorsements; check peer availability and policy membership. Third, commit-time validation failures such as MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) conflicts happen when another transaction changed data between endorsement and commit; the transaction is marked invalid at commit. A common mistake is not distinguishing these cases and offering a generic retry. Instead, inspect the error message and decide: retry, prompt the user to resolve input, or surface a policy configuration issue. In terminal demos, deliberately attempt to re-create an existing asset to observe a chaincode error. Finally, always validate input client-side to reduce malformed payloads reaching chaincode. Error Handling & Common Failures means catch chaincode exceptions, detect endorsement policy failures, and handle mvcc conflicts with application-level logic.. In practical terms, chaincode errors, endorsement policy failures, and mvcc conflicts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Error Handling & Common Failures
Common error types
  • Chaincode error: invalid input or business logic rejects the operation.
  • Endorsement failure: insufficient valid endorsements per policy.
  • MVCC/Validation failure: conflict detected at commit time, transaction invalidated.
Concrete terminal example
Attempting to create asset1 twice will throw an error with a message like: the asset asset1 already exists. Catch it and log appropriately.
Suggested handling
Inspect the error message, classify the cause, and apply the correct response: retry for transient endorsement or ordering delays; prompt user for invalid input; escalate policy failures to operators.
Pro tip
Log full error details server-side but present concise, actionable messages to end users to avoid leaking internal details.
Common mistake

Treating all failures the same. Differentiate chaincode logic errors from endorsement or commit failures before retrying.

screens.title: Responses: Buffer vs No Payload
screens.narratorSegment: The submitTransaction call may return a Buffer containing chaincode data or may resolve with no meaningful payload when chaincode does not return a value. Treat the returned Buffer as opaque binary until you convert it to a string or parse JSON. A common pattern is to check result && result. length and then call toString to log or parse JSON. If your chaincode returns structured JSON, convert the buffer to string and then parse JSON safely. A typical mistake is assuming submitTransaction always returns JSON; sometimes you will get an empty buffer when the chaincode only calls PutState and returns nothing. In that case, rely on 'committed' acknowledgement rather than expecting data. When you design APIs, decide whether chaincode functions should return a summary payload for client convenience or remain void to minimize data transfer. For terminals and automated tests, always log result. toString() or 'committed' when empty so your scripts have clear output. And remember: converting buffers and parsing JSON is a client responsibility; chaincode must document what it returns. screens.title: Input Validation and Security
screens.narratorSegment: Client-side input validation is an important layer of defense. While chaincode should always validate data, validating inputs before calling submitTransaction reduces the chance of sending malformed or malicious payloads into the network. For example, confirm that numeric fields are numeric strings, string lengths are within allowed limits, and required fields are present. This reduces avoidable chaincode errors and helps produce clearer user feedback. It also prevents some classes of malformed data from reaching chaincode where they could cause logic errors. A common misconception is that validation on chaincode is sufficient; in practice a layered approach works best: validate at the client, sanitize again in chaincode, and log violations at both ends. In multi-organization networks, client validation also helps maintain good A P I discipline across different user interfaces. If your application accepts file uploads or complex data, perform strict schema checks and reject bad input early so submitTransaction is used only for legitimate state changes. This keeps your ledger consistent and your user experience predictable. Input validation: client and chaincode
A layered validation approach reduces errors and security risks.
Client-side checks
  • Type and range checks for numeric strings.
  • Required field presence and length limits.
  • Sanitize strings to avoid injection-like issues in application logic.
Chaincode-side validation
  • Defensive checks: existence, ownership, and business rules.
  • Return clear error messages that the client can map to user actions.
Practical guideline
Validate early and reject early. Keep submitTransaction calls limited to well-formed and authorized requests to maintain ledger integrity and predictable behavior.
Key Takeaway

A layered validation strategy reduces runtime errors and makes transaction outcomes easier to reason about for both developers and users.

In this lesson you will learn how a client application invokes chaincode functions that change the ledger. We focus on the Fabric Node. js SDK method that submits transactions and waits until peers commit them, giving your application a strong guarantee that state changes are finalized. You'll see how to obtain the channel network and the contract, how arguments are passed as strings and parsed by chaincode, and why proper error handling matters when endorsement or commit fails. A practical, terminal-style demonstration will guide you through creating and updating assets with a sample basic chaincode and interpreting results returned by the SDK. We'll also highlight common pitfalls like forgetting to convert response buffers, not validating input client-side, and misunderstanding the difference between a query and a transaction. By the end, you'll understand the end-to-end transaction flow from the application perspective and be ready to add submitTransaction calls safely to your client code. Think about a simple shipment record function: you will learn which SDK call to use, how to prepare string arguments, and how to detect endorsement failures so your app can respond correctly.

This chapter teaches four practical skills you can apply immediately when building a Fabric client. First, you'll clearly differentiate submitTransaction and evaluateTransaction and know when to use each: submitTransaction is for state changes that must be committed, evaluateTransaction is for read-only queries. Second, you'll implement submitTransaction calls that create or update ledger entries, including the steps to obtain a Network and Contract object first. Third, you'll learn to pass arguments correctly from Node. js — all arguments should be strings and the chaincode is responsible for parsing types. Fourth, you'll handle transaction responses and errors robustly, converting buffer responses to strings and catching errors caused by chaincode logic, endorsement policy failures, or commit conflicts. Each objective includes a short verification milestone so you can test competency: run a simple app to create an asset, observe the committed result, and handle an expected duplicate-asset error without crashing the client. These skills matter because they make your client predictable, secure, and safe to run in production. Practice these steps in a terminal-based demo to solidify your understanding.

This second objectives screen links each skill to a terminal-based verification. For submit versus evaluate, run a read-only evaluateTransaction first to inspect state, then call submitTransaction to create or update an asset and observe the ledger change. For implementing submitTransaction, test by obtaining gateway. getNetwork and network. getContract, then submit a CreateAsset call and watch the SDK log the commit. For argument passing, pass every parameter as a string and confirm the chaincode parses numeric strings into integers or returns validation errors when malformed. For responses and errors, convert any Buffer response into a string and add try/catch around submitTransaction to capture chaincode errors such as duplicate asset creation or endorsement policy failures. These verification steps matter because real networks surface timing and endorsement differences not visible in theory. Practicing in a terminal makes the asynchronous lifecycle concrete and helps you design robust client-side retry, logging, and user feedback patterns. After running the sample app, reflect on whether your client recovers gracefully from expected failures.

A transaction in Fabric is any operation that intends to change ledger state. From the client perspective, that means you must use submitTransaction rather than evaluateTransaction. submitTransaction initiates a coordinated lifecycle: the SDK assembles and signs a proposal, gets endorsements from peers that simulate the change, and then submits the endorsed transaction to ordering. After ordering, peers validate and commit the block. This end-to-end process gives your application assurance that the effect is durable and visible to other peers. A common misconception is that submitTransaction only sends a write request and exits. In fact, the Node. js SDK waits until peers commit the transaction and will resolve the returned Promise only after that commitment. An example use case is a CreateAsset function: you must submit a transaction so that the new asset appears in the world state across peers. Contrast this with evaluateTransaction, which is appropriate for reads, fast inspection, and does not touch ordering or block formation. When designing applications, treat submitTransaction as a synchronous checkpoint: it is your signal that the change is finalized. Remember to validate input before submission and to prepare for errors from chaincode logic or endorsement mismatches.

Before submitting any transaction you must obtain two references: a Network object representing the channel and a Contract object representing the deployed chaincode. The Gateway connection encapsulates your application identity and discovery settings. From that gateway you call gateway. getNetwork with the channel name to retrieve a Network. Then call network. getContract with the chaincode name — optionally including a contract name within the package — to get a Contract. This mapping matters because the Contract determines the available functions you can call. A common pattern is network. getContract('basic', 'myAssetContract') when using the contract A P I structure inside chaincode. If chaincode exposes functions directly without the contract A P I, you may call network. getContract('basic') and reference functions by name. Verify that the channel name and chaincode name match what was deployed; a mismatch is a frequent source of runtime errors. Practically, you will place these calls after gateway. connect in your Node. js main function and reuse the Contract instance for multiple submitTransaction and evaluateTransaction calls. This reuse reduces overhead and makes your code clearer. Always disconnect the gateway when your app completes.

When you call submitTransaction, the SDK triggers a multi-step lifecycle. First it creates a transaction proposal that includes the chaincode function name and arguments and signs it with your application's identity. Next, endorsing peers receive the proposal and simulate execution, producing signed proposal responses containing read/write sets. The Gateway collects the required endorsements based on the chaincode's endorsement policy. Once enough valid endorsements are collected, the Gateway packages them into a final transaction and submits it to the ordering service. The ordering service sequences transactions and forms blocks. Blocks are distributed to peers, which validate transactions by checking endorsement policy and read/write conflicts, and then commit the valid transactions to the ledger. The Node. js submitTransaction Promise resolves only after peers commit the transaction to their ledgers, providing your application with a durable success signal. A useful mental model is: proposal for simulation, endorsements as signed agreement, ordering for global sequence, and commitment for durable state change. Design your application to handle failures at each stage: endorsement errors, ordering delays, or commit rejections due to MVCC conflicts. submitTransaction Lifecycle means proposal → endorsement → collection → ordering → commitment; submittransaction coordinates these and waits for commit.. Second, endorsement policy failures occur when the collected proposal responses do not satisfy the chaincode's endorsement policy.
